text: The Russo-Ukrainian war turned into a contest of sensor-to-decision-to-strike loops; whichever side closes the loop faster, and denies the other its loop, holds ground at lower cost.
notes: Uncited synthesis in the overview of 05; cites the file's key overview sources as background.

text: Four long trends in ISR, C2 and logistics run through all nine eras of the war: growing battlefield transparency, mass becoming a liability, digital cloud-based Ukrainian C2, and logistics becoming the main target.
Battlefield transparency grew over the war and the drone "kill zone" got deeper.
In 2022 surveillance came mainly from Orlan-10 drones, Bayraktar TB2s, commercial and allied satellites and intercepted radio traffic, and artillery did the killing.
In 2022 Russian units with their own drones could put fire on a target 3–5 minutes after spotting it.

In early 2025 RUSI described a dense drone network: the battlefield was fully visible within 3 km of the line of contact, coverage thinned out to about 15 km, and commanders could task reconnaissance out to about 40 km.

text: In mid-2026 Ukrainian commanders put the zone of regular drone strikes at 20–25+ km on both sides of the line.

observations.note: upper end open (25+); on both sides of the line

text: One Ukrainian corps commander expects the kill zone to reach 30 km by the end of 2026.
Assault groups shrank over the war: from Russian BTG columns in 2022, to Ukrainian assault detachments of 20 or fewer, to Russian infiltration teams of 1–5 people in 2025–26.
Vehicles now hide in dug-in shelters and dart out to fire, and troops walk the last 10–15+ km to positions.

Ukrainian C2 went digital and cloud-based with Starlink as its backbone: Kropyva, GIS Arta, Delta and its modules (Vezha, Avengers AI, Mission Control, Delta Tube) and the ePoints bonus scheme all ride on Starlink and cellular links.

Russia built a C2 system similar to Ukraine's, with Strelets, drone "reconnaissance-fire circuits" and smuggled Starlink terminals, but Russian C2 has been reported as more centralised and more fragile.

In February 2026 a Starlink speed cap (late January) and then SpaceX's whitelist (enforced 5 February) cut off unregistered Starlink terminals, Russian front-line C2 broke down, and Ukraine made its fastest gains since 2023.
Russia partially recovered its C2 over summer 2026 through mesh radios, other satellites, relays and laundered whitelist registrations; the Ukrainian edge narrowed but did not close.
Logistics became the main target of the war.
In 2022 Ukraine used HIMARS against Russian depots.
In 2024 Ukraine used long-range drones against Russian arsenals such as Toropets and Tikhoretsk.
In 2025 Russian drone units such as Rubikon hunted Ukrainian supply roads.
In 2026 a Ukrainian "middle strike" / "Logistics Lockdown" campaign at 20–200 km depth cut freight on the M-14 by about 71% and caused fuel rationing in Crimea.

text: Both sides now net their roads, move at night and hand the last mile to ground robots (UGVs, Ukrainian NRK).
Ukraine logged 25,143 UGV missions in August 2026 alone.

In the 2022 invasion Aerorozvidka, then a volunteer IT-born drone unit, worked with about 30 Ukrainian special-forces troops on quad bikes, with thermal drones and night-vision goggles, to ambush the Russian column north of Kyiv at night.
notes: The unit's own claims were only partly verified.

text: Aerorozvidka's first targets in the night ambushes north of Kyiv were the Russian column's forward supply depot and its lead vehicles; the unit's own claims were only partly verified.
At the start of the 2022 invasion Russian units had no time to exchange radio encryption keys and troops were poorly trained on their radios, so many fell back on stolen civilian phones.
Because of Russian C2 failures in early 2022, Ukraine was able to monitor much of Russian tactical radio traffic.
Only 10–20% of Russian brigade/BTG radio traffic in early 2022 was about combat management; most of it was units reporting their own locations.

text: In early 2022 Russian units reused the same routes and staging areas and relied on a few main supply routes.
In 2022 Ukraine photographed bomb damage at its airfields, printed the pattern onto covers and brought aircraft back to "destroyed" sites, and dummy air-defence sites soaked up Russian munitions.
Russian satellite intelligence missed 3–4 Ukrainian military trains a day in March 2022.

By mid-2022 Russia had already lost at least 1,254 trucks and fuel tankers, according to the Oryx count.

text: In 2022 the Russian kill chain took 3–5 minutes with a unit's own drone; via a fire-control HQ it took 20–30 minutes at tactical level and about 48 hours at operational level.
RUSI notes that in 2022 Russian forces reliably committed resources against Ukraine's telegraphed moves and missed its concealed ones.
The pattern of Russia reacting to telegraphed moves and missing concealed ones fits the loudly advertised Kherson push versus the Kharkiv breakthrough in autumn 2022.

text: Russian battle-damage assessment was weak in 2022: troops were not encouraged to report failures, and data was fused poorly between sensors.
Ukraine used decoys of prestige systems and false radio traffic, and Russian cruise missiles hit dummy HIMARS in August 2022.
Ukrainian MLRS strikes in July 2022 drove Russian headquarters beyond 120 km from the front line, causing serious friction through the autumn.

text: The "People's Satellite" was bought with $13.5 million crowdfunded in three days in June 2022, the "People's Bayraktar" money redirected when Baykar donated the drones.
The ICEYE contract signed on 18 August 2022 gives Ukraine one dedicated SAR satellite plus tasking across the ICEYE constellation.
ICEYE imagery from the People's Satellite reached HUR from September 2022; it sees through cloud and at night, at up to 0.25 m resolution.
A truck bomb on the Crimean Bridge (Kerch) on 8 October 2022 dropped road spans and set fuel tank cars on fire.
After the October 2022 attack, the Crimean Bridge road bridge was fully reopened only in February 2023 and the rail bridge in May 2023.
During the Bakhmut period Russia refined its "reconnaissance-strike complex": the kill chain took 3–5 minutes from drone detection to fires and 20–30 minutes from an electronic-warfare detection.
Strelets, a Russian reconnaissance/fire-control data system, was widely used by VDV (airborne), Wagner and reconnaissance specialists in 2022–23.
In 2022–23 Russia fielded about one major EW system per 10 km of front, sited about 7 km behind the line.

Russian C2 hardened in 2022–23: headquarters dispersed and were wired to forward command posts, often through the captured Ukrainian civilian telecoms network.
Russian brigade command posts sat about 20 km behind the line, underground, in 2022–23.

text: Below battalion level, much Russian traffic was still sent in the clear on analogue radios in 2022–23.
Russia judged massed-fire doctrine unworkable in 2023, partly because "the logistics enabling such a volume of fire is too vulnerable to detection and long-range precision strike".

text: During the 2023 counteroffensive Russia shifted to precision fires against Ukrainian columns: Krasnopol laser-guided shells designated by drones, and Lancets and FPVs flown with reconnaissance drones against lead elements.
Ukrainian gun crews had to displace 2–15 minutes after opening fire in 2023.

Only 3% of Ukrainian fire missions in 2023 were smoke, because smoke blinds the drone feeds that brigade HQs use to manage the fight; commanders preferred to keep their own picture over concealing their troops.

Uncrewed boats struck the Crimean Bridge on 17 July 2023, and a span collapsed.
Ukrainian Defence Intelligence (HUR) confirmed Russian use of Starlink in February 2024; the terminals were reportedly bought through third countries.
RUSI fieldwork in 2024 described a mature "mass observation" battlefield in which Russian combat groups try to keep five drone orbits over each axis of advance.

text: In 2024 each Russian drone orbit streamed over a satellite uplink to battalion and brigade command posts, where the intelligence officer, fires officer and commander's representative authorised strikes.
RUSI found in 2024 that neither side generally uses fire controllers inside combat units.
During the artillery shortage one Ukrainian brigade held 18 km of front with four working howitzers.
Drones filled the Ukrainian artillery gap in 2023–24 and caused 60–70% of damaged or destroyed Russian systems.
In 2023–24, 60–80% of Ukrainian FPVs failed to reach their target.
Ukrainian decoy production grew among volunteers and industry in 2023–24.
Decoy Stugna anti-tank launchers cost $30–100.
Metinvest had made 250+ radar and howitzer decoys by 2024.
Good decoys copy radar, thermal and acoustic signatures and simulate firing or explosions.

After the March 2025 scare, Ukrainian satellite ISR diversified: HUR runs its own platform for French CSO-3 imagery under a deal signed in February 2025.
Japan shares SAR imagery with HUR, its first such sharing with any foreign state, and Germany and Italy provide radar imagery to Ukraine.
NATO's APSS ("Aquila") pools data from 18 nations' satellites.
ICEYE, with 54 SAR satellites, has become the linchpin of Ukrainian satellite ISR; a German-funded contract has supplied SAR data to the Ministry of Defence since November 2024.
Rheinmetall and ICEYE plan to build satellites in Germany.
The crowdfunded "People's Satellite" had delivered 5,900+ SAR images to HUR by May 2026.

text: The volunteer-built Russian Glaz/Groza complex turns a one-click mark on a drone feed into a full fire-mission package for guns and mortars, cutting detection-to-impact from hours to minutes.
Belousov announced the "Svod" tactical situational-awareness complex in August 2025.
A Russian Ministry of Defence council on a unified drone-management system met in September 2025.
In early 2025 a spyware-laced copy of the AlpineQuest mapping app leaked Russian unit locations.

From late December 2025, Rubikon and other Russian units flew Starlink-equipped BM-35 and Molniya-2 drones deep into the Ukrainian rear, hitting trains and traffic on the E-50 highway, much like the battlefield air interdiction that enabled their advances at Pokrovsk and Huliaipole.
The Starlink cutoff of Russian forces came in phases, and the differing dates in the sources describe different steps.

The trigger for the Starlink cutoff (late December 2025 – January 2026) was that Rubikon and other Russian units had fitted Starlink to BM-35 and Molniya-2 drones for strikes deep in the Ukrainian rear, against trains and vehicles on the E-50 Pokrovsk–Pavlohrad highway.
On 29 January 2026 Fedorov said the Ministry of Defence had contacted SpaceX within hours of Starlink-guided Russian drones appearing over Ukrainian cities.
The first step of the Starlink cutoff (late January – 1 February 2026) was a speed-based cutoff for terminals moving faster than about 75–90 km/h, which hit Starlink-equipped Shaheds and Molniyas.
notes: The text gives 'late January'; the 29 January start date comes from 05 §6 ('about 29 Jan–1 Feb').

text: On 1 February 2026 Musk wrote on X that the Starlink steps against Russian drones had worked.
On 1 February 2026 Fedorov announced that only authorised Starlink terminals would be allowed in Ukraine.
On 2 February 2026 a Cabinet resolution set up the Starlink whitelist: civilians register at administrative service centres, businesses via Diia and the military via Delta.
On 5 February 2026 unregistered Starlink terminals went dark at about 03:00 Kyiv time, enforcing the whitelist.
On 5 February 2026 Fedorov said Russian Starlink terminals were blocked and the whitelist was being updated once a day.

ISW and outlets relaying it date the Russian Starlink block to "1 February", meaning the first step, while OSW and the Kyiv Independent date it to 5 February, meaning enforcement; United24's "early December" is an error.
notes: Date reconciliation by the research file.

text: After the Starlink block in February 2026, the Ukrainian General Staff reported fewer Russian assaults, and none at all in some sectors.
After the Starlink block in February 2026, Ukrainian brigades reported fewer Russian FPV sorties and fewer Molniya strikes on the rear.
After losing Starlink, Russian units fell back on radios, cables, Wi-Fi bridges and cellular links, then brought in Yamal/Express satellite terminals and mesh networks.
Roskomnadzor throttled Telegram on 9–10 February 2026, although Russian units used it for horizontal coordination and air-defence cueing.
Peskov said he could not imagine troops using messengers at the front, and Russian milbloggers called that a lie.
After the Starlink cutoff Rubikon stopped posting location details.
After the Starlink cutoff Russian logistics units reportedly dropped Starlink-linked UGVs for crewed trucks and motorcycles.
On 26 February 2026 Brig. Gen. Biletskyi (3rd Army Corps) said the Starlink cutoff had cut Russian drone effectiveness by roughly 20–40% in two weeks.

Biletskyi expected in February 2026 that Russian drone units would partially recover through other satellite links within one to two months, but not return to Starlink-level efficiency for three to five years.

text: Ukraine gained 201 km² in one week after the Starlink cutoff, per ISW data.
Zelensky claimed Ukrainian gains of 745 km² by 12 August 2026.
Ukraine's own Starlink terminals had been pre-registered and were largely unaffected by the whitelist cutoff.
Operation Vivaldi, north of Lyman from the end of May to September 2026, is the best-documented Ukrainian ISR/C2 operation of the year.

The 3rd Army Corps attacked the Russian salient north of Lyman from about the end of May 2026 under an information blackout, and its commander Biletskyi confirmed Operation Vivaldi only on 15 September.
In Operation Vivaldi, SSO, border-guard and HUR units fought under the same tactical command as the 3rd Army Corps.

The 3rd Army Corps claims Operation Vivaldi cleared 75 km² of infiltrators and de-occupied 10 km² in "season" one, then 40 km² more in season two (20 September: Shandryholove, Derylove, Drobysheve), for 125+ km² in all.

In Operation Vivaldi, brigade and corps reconnaissance mapped the Russian command nodes whose loss would break control of the sector, and heavy bomber drones then dropped kamikaze UGVs onto them more than 10 km behind the line.

counter: Starlink whitelist of registered terminals
measure: Russian use of smuggled Starlink terminals for front-line C2 and drones
effect: cut Russian drone effectiveness by roughly 20–40% in two weeks (3rd Army Corps claim)
rationale: From 5 February 2026 unregistered terminals went dark and Fedorov said Russian terminals were blocked; Russian front-line C2 broke down and Biletskyi reported a 20–40% cut in Russian drone effectiveness.

counter: Starlink speed-based cutoff
measure: Starlink-equipped Russian strike drones (Shahed, Molniya, BM-35)
effect: disables terminals moving faster than about 75–90 km/h
rationale: The first step of the cutoff disabled terminals moving faster than about 75–90 km/h, hitting Starlink-equipped Shaheds and Molniyas.

counter: Russian mesh-radio relays (XK-F358 modems, Ubiquiti links)
measure: Starlink whitelist cutoff
effect: restored long-range drone control, 150–175 km by September 2026
rationale: Mesh radio was Russia's second adaptation to losing Starlink; self-healing networks spread to long-range drones after the cutoff, and by September relay chains controlled drones 150–175 km out.

counter: Radio relays, fibre-optic internet links and Kometa satellites for Molniya motherships
measure: Starlink whitelist cutoff
effect: partial substitute; slower than Starlink
rationale: By mid-March 2026 Molniya motherships again carried FPVs 40–50 km deep using these links, slower than Starlink but a partial substitute.

counter: Laundered whitelist registrations through paid Ukrainians
measure: Starlink whitelist
effect: restores Starlink access for some Russian terminals
rationale: Russia paid Ukrainians to register terminals in their own names; SBU cases include 76 terminals for the FSB and a suspect with 1,000+ registrations.

counter: Rassvet LEO constellation
measure: Starlink whitelist cutoff
effect: limited coverage windows (up to about 90 minutes a day by late August 2026)
rationale: Rassvet is the planned Russian Starlink substitute; by late August it had about an hour or more of daily windows, far short of the 200–250 satellites needed for round-the-clock service.

counter: Yamal/Express and Gazprom Space Systems satellite terminals, radios, cable and Wi-Fi bridges
measure: Starlink whitelist cutoff
effect: far less reliable substitutes
rationale: Russian units fell back on these after losing Starlink; Gazprom Space Systems are 'far less reliable'.

counter: Ukrainian strikes on exposed Russian substitute emitters
measure: Large antennas and repeaters on high-rises as Starlink substitutes
effect: emitters expose positions to strikes
rationale: In March 2026 the antennas and repeaters Russian units put on high-rises exposed positions and drew Ukrainian strikes.

counter: Volna Kupol Garant Starlink jammer
measure: Ukrainian Starlink-linked drones and communications
effect: 0–35% packet loss; breaks unhardened drone links
rationale: Kupol deafens passing Starlink satellites over about 20 km², causing 0–35% packet loss, enough to break unhardened drone links.

counter: AI-terminal drones such as the Hornet
measure: Volna Kupol Garant Starlink jamming
effect: unaffected by link jamming
rationale: Drones with terminal AI guidance need no live link and are unaffected by the Kupol jammer.

counter: Ukrainian strikes on Kupol jammers
measure: Volna Kupol Garant Starlink jammer
effect: three Kupol jammers destroyed by August 2026
rationale: The jammer's power makes it a beacon for strikes; a third destroyed Kupol was confirmed at Gelendzhik in August 2026.

counter: Anti-drone net tunnels over supply roads
measure: Russian FPV interdiction of Ukrainian supply roads (Rubikon)
rationale: Ukrainian brigades put up net tunnels after Rubikon arrived near Kostiantynivka; by 2026 vehicles ran at up to 120 km/h under nets, and 1,066 km were built January–July 2026.

counter: Heavy bomber-drone resupply (Kazhan)
measure: Russian drone interdiction of Ukrainian supply roads (Rubikon)
effect: up to 20 resupply runs per crew per day
rationale: With roads under Rubikon fibre-optic FPV attack, Kazhan bomber drones flew food, water, fuel and grenades around the clock.

counter: UGV last-mile logistics
measure: Drone kill zone over supply routes
rationale: Both sides hand the last mile to ground robots; Ukrainian UGV missions, mostly logistics, rose to 25,143 in August 2026 and the General Staff credits UGVs with up to 30% fewer casualties.

counter: Mines, FPV and fibre-optic drones and dedicated Russian UGV-hunting crews
measure: Ukrainian logistics UGVs
effect: UGV lifespan fell from 12–15 to 3–4 missions
rationale: A Khartia commander says UGV lifespan fell from 12–15 missions to 3–4 near Kupiansk from these causes; at 10–15 km/h robots are too slow to cross logistics routes safely.

counter: Russian anti-drone net tunnels and drone-detector 'traffic lights'
measure: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian supply routes
rationale: Russia netted roads (e.g. 2+ km between Bakhmut and Chasiv Yar, February 2025) and placed drone-detector traffic lights along supply routes.

counter: Fibre-optic FPV
measure: EW-based protection against drones
effect: undercuts EW-based protection
rationale: The Russian move to fibre-optic FPVs began to undercut EW-based protection.

counter: HIMARS/GMLRS strikes
measure: Russian rail-fed depots within 30–50 km of the front
rationale: HIMARS wrecked most Russian depots in Donbas and the south within weeks; RUSI calls its arrival the end of the Russian Donbas offensive.

counter: Moving Russian depots beyond HIMARS range (100+ km)
measure: HIMARS/GMLRS strikes on depots
effect: roughly doubles delivery times
rationale: Russia pulled stocks back to 50 and later 100 km; moving depots past the ~85 km range roughly doubles delivery times.

counter: Russian HQ displacement beyond 120 km
measure: Ukrainian MLRS strikes on headquarters
effect: HQs survive but C2 friction rises
rationale: July 2022 MLRS strikes drove Russian HQs beyond 120 km, which caused serious friction through the autumn.

counter: Decoys (dummy HIMARS, M777, air-defence sites)
measure: Russian precision missile strikes
rationale: Decoys costing $30–1,000 drew Russian cruise missiles and Kalibrs costing $3–6M; dummy air-defence sites soaked up munitions.

counter: Ukrainian middle strike / Logistics Lockdown
measure: Russian road logistics on the R-280/M-14 into Crimea
effect: M-14 freight down about 71%
rationale: Middle strike at 20–200 km depth hit 125 trucks in spring 2026 and cut M-14 freight by 71% (Brovdi), with fuel rationing in Crimea.

counter: Russian camouflage, decoys, mobile fire teams, road netting and disguised fuel transport
measure: Ukrainian middle strike
rationale: Russia responded to middle strike with these measures, including moving military fuel in ambulances and bread vans.

counter: Armoured trains and BARS mobile fire teams guarding railways
measure: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian rail logistics
effect: partial; some trains disabled
rationale: Russia brought back armoured trains to escort resupply and repair crews and uses BARS teams to guard railways; drones have disabled some trains.

counter: Air-defence and EW 'dome' over the assault area (Operation Vivaldi)
measure: Russian drone ISR over the Lyman axis
effect: denies the enemy's drones a picture of the attack
rationale: The dome blinded Russian drones so they could not read the operation's design.

counter: Air-dropped kamikaze UGVs and strike drones on mapped command nodes (Operation Vivaldi)
measure: Russian command posts and C2 nodes on the Lyman axis
effect: Russian troops diverted to guard command posts
rationale: Reconnaissance mapped nodes whose loss would break control; strikes forced Russia to pull troops back to guard CPs.

counter: Strikes on both ends of the Voronezh–Luhansk diesel pipeline
measure: Russian pipeline fuel supply to the Lyman axis
effect: fuel moved to a 400 km truck run; drone generators could not be refuelled
rationale: Strikes forced Russia to dismantle the pipeline, which had supplied about 50% of daily fuel; fuel now goes on a 400 km truck run.

counter: Russian EW decryption of radio traffic
measure: Ukrainian Motorola radio communications
effect: near-real-time decryption
rationale: Russian EW reportedly decrypted Ukrainian Motorola traffic in near real time.

counter: Ukrainian interception of Russian tactical radio
measure: Russian unencrypted analogue radios and civilian phones
rationale: With no encryption keys and poorly trained operators, Russian traffic could be monitored by Ukraine.

counter: European and Japanese satellite ISR (CSO-3, ICEYE, Japanese SAR, APSS)
measure: US suspension of GEGD Maxar imagery
effect: partial; dependence on US imagery remains
rationale: After the March 2025 suspension Ukraine diversified satellite ISR, though Budanov still called Kyiv critically dependent on US imagery in December 2025.

counter: Gun displacement within 2–15 minutes of firing
measure: Russian drone-cued precision counter-fire
rationale: Ukrainian gun crews had to displace 2–15 minutes after opening fire under Russian precision fires designated by drones.

counter: Night and bad-weather rotations spaced more than a month apart
measure: Persistent Russian drone surveillance of the rear
rationale: Rotations were run at night and in bad weather because about half of Ukrainian casualties were taken in the rear during rotation and resupply.
